title: Shannon's Sampling Theorem: Why Twice the Highest Frequency?

paper.title: Communication in the Presence of Noise

hook: A sine wave sampled too slowly looks like a slower sine wave. This is aliasing. Shannon's theorem tells us exactly how fast we must sample to avoid it.

symbols.meaning: Integer chosen so that f_a is in [0, f_s/2]

equation.caption: The apparent frequency after sampling. If f_s > 2f, then k=0 and f_a = f (no aliasing). If f_s < 2f, k≥1 and f_a < f (aliasing).

steps: Signal: x(t) = \sin(2\pi f t) with f = {{f}} Hz.
Sampling rate: f_s = {{fs}} Hz. Nyquist rate: 2f = {{fN}} Hz.
Apparent frequency: f_a = |f - k f_s| = {{fa}} Hz.
If f_s > 2f, then k=0 and f_a = f. If f_s < 2f, then k≥1 and f_a < f.

explorations.title: No aliasing when sampling above Nyquist
explorations.predict: Set f = 3 Hz and f_s = 10 Hz. Is f_s > 2f? What is f_a?
explorations.observe: f_s = 10 Hz > 2f = 6 Hz. k = round(3/10) = 0. f_a = |3 - 0| = 3 Hz. The apparent wave matches the original.
explorations.why: Because f_s > 2f, the sampling rate is high enough to capture the signal's oscillations. The alias index k is 0, so f_a = f.

explorations.title: Aliasing when sampling below Nyquist
explorations.predict: Set f = 7 Hz and f_s = 10 Hz. Is f_s > 2f? What is f_a?
explorations.observe: f_s = 10 Hz < 2f = 14 Hz. k = round(7/10) = 1. f_a = |7 - 10| = 3 Hz. The apparent wave is slower (3 Hz) than the original (7 Hz).
explorations.why: Because f_s < 2f, the samples cannot distinguish the 7 Hz signal from a 3 Hz signal. The alias index k=1 gives f_a = |f - f_s| = 3 Hz.

self_tests.name: Nyquist rate is twice the signal frequency
Apparent frequency never exceeds half the sampling rate

limitation: This demonstration uses a single sine wave. Shannon's theorem applies to any bandlimited signal, but here we only show the simplest case. Also, we assume ideal sampling (instantaneous samples) and perfect reconstruction, which ignores practical issues like finite sampling aperture and quantization.
misconception: A common misconception is that sampling faster than the signal frequency is enough. In fact, you must sample faster than twice the highest frequency to avoid aliasing.

claims.text: A signal must be sampled at a rate greater than twice its highest frequency to be reconstructed without aliasing.
When sampling below the Nyquist rate, the apparent frequency is |f - k f_s| for some integer k.
The toy model uses a single sine wave and ideal sampling to illustrate the theorem.

outcomes.outcome: Explain why the sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency.
Compute the apparent frequency when aliasing occurs.
Identify when aliasing happens by comparing f_s and 2f.
